# Why ATMA Commands Appear Successful but Return No Data on OBDII

When debugging vehicle telemetry, it is frustrating to receive an `OK` response from your ECU while expecting a stream of live diagnostic frames. You connect a terminal app to the OBD-II port, send standard P0171 or speed requests, and watch them execute flawlessly. Then you issue the `ATMA` command to monitor all CAN traffic, hoping to see the raw bus activity dump onto your screen. Instead, the ELM327 adapter replies with `OK`, pauses for a new instruction, and remains silent on the data stream.

This specific failure mode is almost exclusively an implementation detail of the OBD-II protocol itself, not a hardware defect in your Ford Figo or the ELM327 chip. To understand why this happens, you must distinguish between OBD-II PIDs and CAN frame monitoring.

The `ATMA` command is designed to force the adapter to act as a transparent bridge, forwarding every message it receives on the physical bus to the host interface (your Android app). While standard diagnostic commands like `ATSP1` or `AT04` query specific Parameter IDs defined by ISO 14229 and return a structured response, `ATMA` does not generate responses. It simply passes data through. If your terminal application expects every command to result in an immediate JSON payload or a string of hex characters, the lack of a "return value" for the monitoring session will look like a failure until you realize no such thing is expected.

In the context of your Ford Figo Diesel connected via HyperTerminal, the behavior you are observing is actually correct according to the ELM327 specification. The adapter successfully entered monitor mode, as evidenced by the `OK` acknowledgement. However, the subsequent silence indicates that either no new CAN frames are arriving on the bus at that specific moment, or the terminal app is not configured to display raw, unstructured hex dumps in real-time.

When you send a standard PID request, such as `AT04 01`, the ECU processes the query and sends back a specific response packet (e.g., engine RPM). This creates a request-response cycle that your app can parse easily. `ATMA` breaks this cycle by entering passive listening mode. The device stops asking questions and starts only echoing whatever the network is shouting. If the vehicle's CAN bus is currently idle regarding non-OBD traffic, or if the OBD gateway within the vehicle only allows specific diagnostic messages through to the ELM327 while filtering out raw internal control frames, your terminal will see nothing but `OK` followed by a prompt for the next command.

Furthermore, many mobile terminal applications, including third-party HyperTerminal clones, have limited support for continuous binary streams when in monitor mode. They are optimized for interactive debugging where you type, wait, and read. Continuous streaming of raw CAN frames often requires a dedicated logger application or a custom implementation using Socket TCP/IP to handle the high-volume data influx without blocking the user interface.

If you require actual visibility into the full CAN bus traffic for your Ford Figo, switching from `ATMA` to a logging mode might yield better results in your specific app environment. Commands like `ATS1` or `ATSB` (Start Logging) often trigger file-based recording that can be dumped later and analyzed with tools like Wireshark or CANoe, bypassing the limitations of real-time text display in a generic terminal emulator. This approach ensures you capture every frame regardless of whether your immediate UI can render it instantly.

Ultimately, the `OK` response confirms the adapter is functioning correctly; the absence of data is a protocol characteristic where transparency yields no immediate feedback loops.
